analysis.one_liner: Bans contracts that gag workers about workplace harassment and ends employers' tax deductions for harassment settlements.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan workplace-harassment bill with 14 cosponsors was sent to six House committees the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or a vote in any of them, and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The EMPOWER Act would make it illegal for an employer to require a worker or job applicant to sign a nondisclosure or nondisparagement clause covering workplace harassment as a condition of getting or keeping a job, and would ban enforcing such clauses. It would explicitly preserve every worker's right to report harassment to the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, state agencies, law enforcement, and the courts regardless of anything they signed. It would also create a confidential EEOC tip-line to detect patterns of harassment at the same employer, require public companies to disclose the number and dollar value of harassment settlements in their annual reports, and change tax law: employers could no longer deduct harassment judgments, related legal costs, or liability insurance, while workers would no longer pay income tax on harassment settlements.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and job applicants, especially the large share of employees who have been or would be asked to sign agreements that could silence them about harassment or discrimination. Harassment victims gain the right to report to any government agency or court no matter what they signed, and settlement money would no longer be taxed as income. Bystanders and coworkers at companies with repeat problems would gain a confidential channel to flag patterns to the EEOC. Investors and the public would see, in company annual reports, how much employers are paying out in harassment settlements.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it an unlawful employment practice for an employer to require, as a condition of employment or promotion, a nondisclosure or nondisparagement clause that covers workplace harassment, and bars employers from enforcing such clauses.
Preserves a worker's or applicant's right to report harassment to the EEOC, state fair-employment agencies, law enforcement, and federal courts, notwithstanding any clause they signed.
Bars employers from unilaterally inserting a one-sided nondisclosure clause that solely benefits the employer into a separation or settlement agreement.

Directs the EEOC to establish a confidential tip-line that collects reports of harassment from employees, applicants, and bystanders, and flags employers with patterns of multiple complaints for potential investigation.

Requires the SEC to write a rule obliging public companies to disclose in their annual reports the number and total dollar amount of workplace-harassment settlements and judgments, including repeat settlements tied to the same individual.
Excludes harassment and discrimination judgments and settlements from the recipient's taxable income and allows backpay awards to be averaged over multiple years for tax purposes.
Denies employers a federal tax deduction for amounts paid under harassment judgments, for related legal and litigation expenses, and for insurance covering such liability.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, above all large companies, would bear the cost: they could no longer condition jobs on silence about harassment, would face litigation exposure from enforcing such clauses, would lose tax deductions for harassment judgments, legal fees, and the insurance covering that liability, and would have to count and disclose settlement payments in public filings. Shareholders would see those payouts disclosed.

drawbacks.text: Nondisclosure clauses remain lawful in settlement or separation agreements that resolve existing legal claims when both sides agree, so an employer can still pay a worker with an accrued claim for silence — the bill stops the gag at hiring, not always at settlement.

The EEOC tip-line is not anonymous, and it only has to operate in a fiscal year with at least $1.5 million appropriated; below $1 million the Commission is not required to run it at all, leaving the program dependent on future funding decisions.

The denial of tax deductions reaches litigation expenses, attorney's fees, and liability insurance as well as the judgment itself, raising the cost for any employer that fights a harassment claim in court and loses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — a worker cannot be required to trade silence about harassment for a job — is substantial and straightforward, and the tax changes simply shift the cost of harassment from workers and taxpayers to the employers responsible. The honest tradeoffs are narrower than the bill's reach: the settlement carve-out leaves the familiar paid-for-silence deal intact once a claim exists, and the tip-line's value depends entirely on Congress actually appropriating money for it. A design question an honest supporter would acknowledge is that eliminating the deduction for contested litigation costs could raise the price of defending even weak or disputed claims.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to six House committees the day it was introduced, and none of them ever took it up, so it expired when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 17, 2018 by Rep. Lois Frankel with three other original cosponsors, including two Republicans, Rep. Ted Poe and Rep. Barbara Comstock.
It gathered 14 cosponsors, split evenly between 7 Republicans and 7 Democrats.

The Speaker referred it to six committees — Education and the Workforce, Ways and Means, Financial Services, House Administration, Oversight and Government Reform, and Judiciary — 'for a period to be subsequently determined.'
The action history shows no hearings, no markups, no committee votes, and no floor action of any kind after the initial referral; the last entry is the July 17, 2018 referral.
The bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, without a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers kept the ability to condition jobs and raises on nondisclosure clauses covering harassment, kept the tax deduction for harassment judgments and the insurance covering them, and avoided public disclosure of settlement counts and payouts. The bill's backers gained nothing from this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers keeping gag clauses and tax deductions

industries.note: The bill bars conditioning jobs or promotions on nondisclosure or nondisparagement clauses covering harassment and denies tax deductions for harassment judgments, legal costs, and liability insurance. Its interest in keeping silence purchasable runs directly against workers' ability to report.

They would have had to disclose in annual filings the number and dollar total of harassment settlements and repeat settlements involving the same individual, exposing a cost most currently bury in legal budgets.
The bill denies a deduction for insurance covering harassment litigation liability, weakening demand for that coverage and raising the effective price of the protection employers buy.
